<reason>Both sides were skilled and well-grounded with no fake sourcing, but A built the more durable route. A's core mechanism — the disclosure default deters self-referrers before any care happens — survived every round, and A pressed it consistently: all of B's harms (unmonitored medication, hallway crises, uncontested claims) sit inside treatment that the status quo prevents. B's best narrowing move (opt-in confidentiality vs blanket default) was real, but A's Q1 exposed that an intake exception only protects patients who arrive, and B's answer leaned back on campus/self-pay routes A had already damaged. B's severe-case argument was badly hurt by A's closing turn on B4.3: if the sickest "do not self-refer under any billing regime" and arrive via family observation, then confidential billing costs B none of those patients, while B's regime additionally loses the treatable self-referrer. B's downstream-blindness reply was rhetorically strong but mechanistically weak, since family noticing never depended on EOBs. B also kept a live, genuinely troubling point on appeals/collections, but it is administrative next to non-treatment. B's clipped Rebuttal 1 was an additional execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing exploitation of B4.3's concession that severe patients never self-refer under any billing regime — collapsing B's weighing by showing the severe arrive identically under both regimes while B's default abandons the self-referrer — capped by the earlier unanswered Q1 pressure that B's "targeted exception" protects only patients the disclosure default already kept from the door.</best_rebuttal>
